# Privatization 101 
## Step 1 - Manufacture a Crisis 
Convince the public that government-run services are slow, broken, and inefficient. All you have to do is highlight a few bad examples and then you just call the whole system broken.

## Step 2 - Starve the public 
Starve the public system of funding. Defund schools, cut social programs, let infrastructure crumble. Force people to beg for private investment. 

## Step 3 - Profit 
Sell off the broken system to private investors. 

# We interrupt this program to bring you 
I understand the appeal of quick dopamine-hit short-form viral media, but the fight that needs to be put up **will not be waged by the members of our society who cannot maintain sustained attention** on the problems that matter. It will not be waged by the members of our society who do not have it within them to do the tedious, necessary work that is required to be a citizen. Someone with a bias for action and a sustained attention span. 

A consumer would be glad for hush money they weren’t expecting. A consumer doesn’t demand transparency. They buy what they are told to buy, and they see only what they are told to see. Be more than a consumer. 

# A Very Brief History of Privatization 
Think tanks and political architects laid the groundwork and built the national narrative for large-scale privatization in the United States several decades ago. 

>Keep think tanks like Heritage, Cato, Reason in mind here. 

## Reagan’s Playbook 
In the 70s, financial emergencies in major cities gave conservatives an opening to push privatization udner the guise of cost cutting and fiscal responsibility. When Regan took power, theory became practice: slash funding, call services inefficient, and offer private solutions. 

>Conservatives tend to reinforce this narrative via assigning keywords such as “waste”, “inefficiency” to government functions. 

Another narrative gained traction in the 80s in Reagan’s terms: Libraries and parks aren’t public goods because only some people use them. This framed citizens as consumers who weren’t getting a return on their tax investment. Government workers were called bureaucrats; social services were called handouts. 

# Public-Private Takeover
If we don’t invest in water as a public good, we will pay for anyway. We’re going to pay for it in higher costs, we’re going to pay for it in environmental damage, we’re going to pay for it in catastrophic public health failures, and corporations will keep finding ways to profit from a resource that should be guaranteed for all.

# Intergenerational Theft 
Disinvestment in public resources and social services may not harm better-off young people today. But it will disproportionately harm future generations who will foot the bill for disinvestment today.
